verses.1: Take up a lamentation for the leaders of Israel.
verses.2: Say, “What was your mother like, O lioness, that lay among lions, gave birth to cubs in the midst of lions?
verses.3: One of her cubs became a lion, learning to tear and to devour people.
verses.4: The nations heard of him; in their pride they captured him and led him off to Egypt in a cage.
verses.5: When she saw that her hope was gone, her expectation lost, she took another of her cubs and made him a lion.
verses.6: He prowled among lions, became a lion himself, learning to tear and to devour people.
verses.7: He devastated widows and cities, and the land and all in it were silenced by the sound of his roar.
verses.8: The surrounding nations closed in on him, cast their nets over him, and in their pride they captured him.
verses.9: They put him in a cage and led him to the king of Babylon, brought him into prison, so that his voice would no longer be heard on the hills of Israel.
verses.10: Your mother was like a vine planted by water, bearing fruit and flourishing with many branches.
verses.11: She had strong branches, like rods for rulers, and her height towered above the trees. In her many branches, she was seen as magnificent.
verses.12: But she was uprooted in anger, cast to the ground, and the scorching wind dried up her fruit. Her branches were stripped and withered, consumed by fire.
verses.13: Now she is planted in the desert, in a dry and thirsty land.
verses.14: Fire came out from her chosen branches and devoured her. There was no strong rod left in her to rule—she is a lament and becomes a lament.

notes:
Notes
- v. 10: The metaphor of the vine is consistent with the broader poetic structure, which alternates between the lioness and the vine to depict the rise and fall of Israel's leadership.
- v. 13: “dry and thirsty land” reflects the Hebrew phrase describing a barren and desolate place, used to emphasize the downfall of the vine.
raw:
[1] Take up a lamentation for the leaders of Israel.

[2] Say, “What was your mother like, O lioness, that lay among lions, gave birth to cubs in the midst of lions?

[3] One of her cubs became a lion, learning to tear and to devour people.

[4] The nations heard of him; in their pride they captured him and led him off to Egypt in a cage.

[5] When she saw that her hope was gone, her expectation lost, she took another of her cubs and made him a lion.

[6] He prowled among lions, became a lion himself, learning to tear and to devour people.

[7] He devastated widows and cities, and the land and all in it were silenced by the sound of his roar.

[8] The surrounding nations closed in on him, cast their nets over him, and in their pride they captured him.

[9] They put him in a cage and led him to the king of Babylon, brought him into prison, so that his voice would no longer be heard on the hills of Israel.

[10] Your mother was like a vine planted by water, bearing fruit and flourishing with many branches.

[11] She had strong branches, like rods for rulers, and her height towered above the trees. In her many branches, she was seen as magnificent.

[12] But she was uprooted in anger, cast to the ground, and the scorching wind dried up her fruit. Her branches were stripped and withered, consumed by fire.

[13] Now she is planted in the desert, in a dry and thirsty land.

[14] Fire came out from her chosen branches and devoured her. There was no strong rod left in her to rule—she is a lament and becomes a lament.

---
Notes
- v. 10: The metaphor of the vine is consistent with the broader poetic structure, which alternates between the lioness and the vine to depict the rise and fall of Israel's leadership.
- v. 13: “dry and thirsty land” reflects the Hebrew phrase describing a barren and desolate place, used to emphasize the downfall of the vine.
